Subject: I am sorry, Salma

Dear Salma,

I have to tell you what I did. Three months ago I put a small amount into an app, and within a week it paid a small profit. It felt like proof. So I put in a larger amount, then more, and I told you and two others to try it. Every time I wanted to stop, I thought: I have already put in so much, I cannot leave now. Yesterday I tried to withdraw and it asked for another fee. I now see that the first payout was the bait, and I brought you into it.

Please stop paying anything. Tomorrow I will go to the bank and report it, and I will tell my parents.

Ritu

qa.q: What happened when Ritu tried to withdraw yesterday?
qa.a: The app asked for another fee when Ritu tried to withdraw.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel each time Ritu wanted to stop paying?
qa.a: Ritu felt trapped, thinking so much had already been put in that leaving was impossible, so Ritu kept paying.

qa.q: What could Salma do after reading the email, and why?
qa.a: Salma could stop paying, keep the messages and tell a trusted adult, because more payments only add to the loss.

qa.q: How might Salma feel on learning that Ritu brought Salma in?
qa.a: Salma may feel worried and perhaps upset, but Ritu's honest warning gives a chance to stop before more is lost.

grounding: A first small payout from a fake app builds trust, so the person invests more and recruits others, and sunk cost keeps the paying going.

You want to know how it started, Nikita? With ₹500. That's what gets me.
I'm Yamini. Last year a girl in my coaching class showed me an app that paid commission for 'rating products'. I put in ₹500 to try it. Next day there was ₹560 in my wallet, and I actually withdrew it. Real money, in my bank. That's when I trusted it.
So I put in ₹5,000. Then ₹20,000 from my savings to unlock 'VIP tasks'. Then I got my cousin and two friends to join, because I thought I was helping them. When withdrawals started saying 'processing', they asked for a 'tax fee' of ₹8,000. I paid, because I'd already put so much in and couldn't stand to lose it.
It never came back. Not mine, not theirs. That first ₹60 was the bait. I just didn't see it.
My cousin still won't talk about it. In March my parents and I reported it all to the cybercrime helpline.

qa.q: How much did Yamini first put in?
Why did Yamini pay the ₹8,000 'tax fee'?
qa.a: Yamini was desperate not to lose what was already in, so the fear of losing everything kept the payments going.

qa.q: What could Yamini have done when withdrawals first said 'processing'?
qa.a: Stopped paying right there, saved the screenshots and told a parent and the bank, instead of paying to free money that was already stuck.

qa.q: What is it like for Yamini's cousin?
qa.a: The cousin trusted Yamini's word, lost money too and still won't talk about it, so the hurt spread beyond one person.

grounding: Shows a small first payout from a fake app building trust until the person invests more, recruits others and keeps paying fees.

I'm Ritu, and Preeti has been my desk-mate at the call centre for a year. I watched this happen over about three months.
It began in June, when she showed me a ₹200 credit from an 'investment app'. 'It actually pays,' she said, glowing. In July she was putting in bigger amounts, ₹10,000, then ₹25,000, and she asked me to join. I didn't. She got two other girls from our floor to sign up.
In August she was on her phone every break, face tight. The app wouldn't let her withdraw unless she paid a 'release charge'. She paid it. Then there was another one. 'I can't stop now,' she told me. 'I've already put in too much.'
In September the team lead noticed her crying and sat with her, and that afternoon they called her brother and the cybercrime helpline together. She stopped paying. I don't know how much she lost in the end. She hasn't said, and I haven't asked.

qa.q: How much was the first credit Preeti showed Ritu?
What does 'I can't stop now' suggest about how Preeti felt?
qa.a: Preeti seemed trapped and desperate, afraid that stopping meant accepting the loss of everything already paid.

qa.q: What else could have helped Preeti earlier, in August?
qa.a: Stopping at the first 'release charge' and telling a trusted adult or the helpline straight away, since fees to withdraw are a common scam sign.

qa.q: How does the whole thing look to Ritu?
qa.a: Ritu watches a friend go from glowing to tight-faced, stays out of it, and respects what Preeti chooses not to share. 🤍

grounding: Shows a small early payout from a fake app building trust, leading to larger payments, recruiting colleagues and paying release charges.
